title: Keep VAT off electricity after March 2027
headline: HMRC’s zero rate ends in March 2027. Keeping it costs about £1.9bn a year.
description: The government took VAT off domestic electricity in Great Britain from 1 October 2026 and put the cost at about £850 million for 2026-27, paid for by cancelling the Digital ID programme. HMRC’s notice says the zero rate is temporary and ends on 31 March 2027, so electricity goes back to 5% in April unless the Budget extends it. This card keeps the rate at 0%: twice the government’s six-month figure, which is our arithmetic, grown with the OBR’s VAT forecast from 2026-27. The Treasury has promised updated costs at the Budget; when they are published they replace this term.

baselinePolicy.text: Domestic fuel and power pay the 5% reduced rate in the March 2026 forecast. The temporary zero rate for electricity in Great Britain runs from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027 and is not in the baseline; the game lists it among the decisions taken since March.

source.quote: The temporary zero rate applies from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027.

terms.label: The government’s cost of the zero rate for the six months from 1 October 2026

source.quote: This action is estimated to cost around £850 million in 2026-27 on the basis of estimated electricity prices. Updated costs will be set out at Budget.

terms.label: Two half-years in a full year, negative because receipts fall

source.quote: The temporary zero rate applies from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027.

rawSource.note: The government published one figure, about £850 million for the six months to March 2027. A full year is taken as twice that, which is our arithmetic, and grown with the OBR’s VAT receipts from 2026-27. Effects before the start year are not applied.

caveats: Annualising the six-month figure is ours. October to March is the high-use half of the year, so twice the winter cost probably overstates a full year; the Treasury has said updated costs will be set out at the Budget, and they replace this term when published.
Great Britain only, as the zero rate is; Northern Ireland stays at 5% under the Windsor Framework arrangements HMRC describes.
Static: no change in electricity use is allowed for, and HMRC’s relief figures carry no behavioural response.

considerations.text: Cheaper electricity means a little more of it is used, and the shift from gas to heat pumps and electric cars raises the base the relief sits on year by year; the card grows with VAT receipts overall, not with electricity demand.

The government put the saving at about £45 a year on a price-cap bill. It is a flat share of every bill, so it is worth more in cash to bigger users and more as a share of income to poorer households.

interactions.text: The gas card’s arithmetic treats electricity as zero-rated for good. Without this card, electricity returns to 5% in April 2027 while gas stays at 0%.
The reduced-rate slider moves the 5% rate on all domestic fuel and power; with electricity at 0% it reaches gas and other fuels only, so the two together overstate.
